name: Places of the Bangsamoro
note: Places worth the journey in BARMM: the travel guide’s own 21, and more each traced to its sources. Photos are Wikimedia Commons files, or English Wikipedia files where a building cannot go to Commons, under free licences.

items.name: Sultan Haji Hassanal Bolkiah Masjid
items.summary: One of the largest mosques in the Philippines, on the edge of the city at Kalanganan.
detail: Four minarets, a gold central dome and a prayer hall built to hold several thousand people, standing in open ground on the western edge of the city. It was funded by the Sultan of Brunei, whose name it carries, and opened in 2011.

The scale is the point and photographs undersell it — the approach across the forecourt is what registers. Inside, the ornament is restrained: geometry and calligraphy, no figures, in the way of the tradition.
It is a working congregational mosque, busiest at Friday midday prayer, and it is used by the city rather than maintained as a monument.

A rehabilitation paid for by the Office of the Chief Minister was handed over on 1 July 2025: waterproofing, repainting, air-conditioning, a new office building and a perimeter fence. The Bangsamoro heritage commission now manages the mosque, which hosts congregational prayers, janazah rites and weddings, and visitors are asked to keep proper decorum inside.
before_you_go: Dress covered — long trousers or a long skirt, shoulders covered. Women are generally expected to cover their hair inside; bring a scarf.
Shoes come off before the prayer hall.
Avoid the hour around Friday midday prayer unless you are attending.
Ask before photographing people, and do not photograph anyone praying.
items.getting_there: In Barangay Kalanganan II, on the western edge of Cotabato City.
items.best_time: December. Mother Kalanganan, the barangay around the mosque, holds the Layagan crab festival every December, and on 19 December 2025 the Shariff Kabunsuan Festival's Guinakit fluvial parade set off from the Mother Kalanganan boulevard.

do.title: Visit the mosque outside prayer times, dressed modestly
do.detail: Cover arms and legs, bring a headscarf if you are a woman, take your shoes off before the prayer hall and stay away during Friday midday prayer unless you are attending.

do.title: See the gold domes and the 43-metre minarets lit at night
do.detail: The minarets are 43 metres high and lit after dark, bright enough to guide pilots flying near the city.

do.title: Watch the sunset from the Baywalk near the mosque
do.detail: A waterfront walk close to the Grand Mosque is where people in the city go to watch the sun set over the bay.

do.title: Look back at the mosque from the Timako Hill bridge
do.detail: The bridge at Timako Hill gives a wide view over Barangay Kalanganan II with the Grand Mosque behind it.

do.title: See brassware made in Kalanganan
do.detail: A Cotabato City guide lists the brassware producers of Barangay Kalanganan among the city's sights; ask locally which workshops take visitors.

eat.title: Mud crab from the Kalanganan fishponds
eat.detail: Kalanganan's fishponds produce hundreds of tons of crab a year, enough for the barangay to call itself a crab capital; mud crab is the dish to ask for nearby.

items.name: Pedro Colina Hill
items.summary: The rock the city was built around, and the view over the Rio Grande delta.
detail: A limestone outcrop rising out of otherwise flat delta country, which is exactly why everyone who has held this city has fortified it — the Maguindanao sultanate before the Spanish, the Spanish after them, and the Philippine constabulary that gave it the name people still use.
The climb is short. What you get at the top is the whole geography of the place at once: the Rio Grande de Mindanao winding out to Illana Bay, the city below, and the Maguindanao plain behind it.
before_you_go: Parts of the hill are occupied by government and security installations; stay on the public approach.
Best in the late afternoon, both for the light and the heat.
items.getting_there: In the city centre: the hill rises behind Tantawan Park at the corner of Quezon and Sinsuat avenues.
items.best_time: Late afternoon, for the light and the heat (the guide's own advice).

do.detail: Since 2018 the houses on this side of the hill have been painted in bright colours with gongs, crabs and guinakit boats, behind the big Cotabato City sign at the corner of Sinsuat and Notre Dame Avenues.

do.title: Climb to the top for the view over the delta
do.detail: Tantawan, the hill's Maguindanaon name, means 'extensive view'; the climb is short, and late afternoon is the best time for both the light and the heat.

do.title: Start at Tantawan Park at the foot of the hill
do.detail: The park with the Sultan Kudarat monument sits at the base of the hill, so it makes a natural starting point for the walk up.

eat.title: Halo-halo at Cafe Le Sorelle
eat.detail: A homegrown cafe on Sinsuat Avenue (Sema Building, corner Macapagal Street) known for chicken, pasta and cheesecake; guides also name its halo-halo a la Sorelle and mais con yelo.

items.name: Kutawato Caves
items.summary: A cave system running under Pedro Colina Hill, and the origin of the city’s name.
detail: "Kutawato" is kuta wato — stone fort — and the caves under the hill are the reason the name stuck. They run beneath the outcrop in the middle of a working city, which is a strange thing to stand in.

The chambers have been used as shelter, as burial space and, in the twentieth century, during wartime. Development around the hill has affected access over the years and the state of the entrances varies.
before_you_go: Ask locally about current access before making the trip; it has opened and closed repeatedly.
Take a guide and a torch. This is not a lit tourist cave.
items.getting_there: At the foot of Pedro Colina Hill in the city proper; Wikipedia lists four entrances, including the Provincial Capitol Cave and the Caverna Espanol.

do.title: Go into the caves with a guide and a torch
do.detail: The cave is not lit for visitors and access has opened and closed over the years, so ask locally about current access before you go.

do.title: Ask which of the four entrances is open
do.detail: The cave system has four named entrances: the Provincial Capitol Cave, Bagua Cave, Caverna Español and Kuweba ni Satur.

eat.title: Dim sum at Las Hermanas
eat.detail: Las Hermanas on Sinsuat Avenue serves siomai and dim sum, with pork-free dishes on the menu.

items.name: Tamontaka Church
items.summary: A nineteenth-century Jesuit mission church, and one of the oldest in Mindanao.
detail: Built for a mission settlement on the Tamontaka river in the 1870s, and a reminder that Cotabato has been a meeting point rather than a monoculture for a very long time. The Christian community here predates the American period.
It is modest architecture and the interest is historical rather than visual, but it sits well against the Grand Mosque a few kilometers away as a way of reading what this city actually is.
before_you_go: A working parish. Around Mass times, attend or come back later.
items.getting_there: In Barangay Tamontaka, on the river at the southern edge of the city; a visitor driving in from General Santos stopped here on the outskirts before reaching the centre. Multicabs and tricycles cover the city.
items.best_time: December 1 to 8, when the city keeps the Feast of the Immaculate Conception, its patron and the dedication of this parish church.

do.title: See the old Jesuit mission church on the Tamontaka River
do.detail: The mission was founded in 1872, the church moved to its present site in 1879, and it was declared a National Historic Landmark in 2004.

do.title: Attend Mass, or come back after it
do.detail: It is a working parish, so around Mass times either join the service or return later.

do.title: Pair it with the Grand Mosque on the same day
do.detail: The church is a few kilometres from the Grand Mosque, and seeing both shows the two faiths that have shared the city for a long time.

eat.title: Fried hito at Babo Katips in Tamontaka
eat.detail: A restaurant in Tamontaka known for its fried catfish (hito).

items.name: Tantawan Park
items.summary: A small historical park at the foot of Pedro Colina Hill, with a monument to Sultan Muhammad Kudarat.
detail: Tantawan Park sits on the corner of Quezon Avenue and Sinsuat Avenue, beside a branch of the Central Bank and the Immaculate Conception Cathedral. Its centrepiece is a monument to Sultan Muhammad Kudarat of Maguindanao.

The ground has a long history. A Maguindanao watchtower stood here to defend the sultanate against Spanish attacks from 1635 to 1645, and it is named as the spot where Shariff Kabunsuan is believed to have docked on the journey that brought Islam to central Mindanao.
The Shariff Kabunsuan Festival each December re-enacts his arrival by river, which makes the park a natural first stop on a walk that takes in the hill and the caves above it.
before_you_go: A public park in the busy city centre; there is nothing to book.
Combine it with Pedro Colina Hill and the Kutawato Caves, which are at the same spot.
items.getting_there: On the corner of Quezon Avenue and Sinsuat Avenue in central Cotabato City.
items.best_time: December 15 to 19, during the Shariff Kabunsuan Festival, which re-enacts his arrival.

do.title: See the monument to Sultan Muhammad Kudarat
do.detail: The park's centrepiece is a monument to the Maguindanao sultan, at the corner of Quezon Avenue and Sinsuat Avenue.

do.title: Get a short massage in the park
do.detail: A 2018 visitor found short, cheap massages on offer in the park.

do.title: Watch the Shariff Kabunsuan Festival in December
do.detail: The festival runs on December 15 to 19, with a dance parade, a boat race and a re-enactment of Shariff Kabunsuan's arrival.

do.title: Walk on up Pedro Colina Hill
do.detail: The hill and the Kutawato Caves are at the same spot, so the park is the first stop on a short walk that takes in all three.

eat.title: Grilled meats on Sinsuat Avenue at night
eat.detail: The barbecue stalls near Rizal Park on Sinsuat Avenue are busy after dark, with several vendors grilling along the road; a must for anyone on a budget.

items.name: Bangsamoro Government Center
items.summary: The seat of the Bangsamoro regional government, with the Bangsamoro Museum inside its cultural complex.
detail: The complex in Rosary Heights holds the offices of the Wali and the Chief Minister, the Bangsamoro Parliament and the regional ministries. Its main building went up in 1976 as the office of the regional governor and earned the nickname Little Malacañan of the South.
For a visitor the reason to come is the Shariff Kabunsuan Cultural Complex, which hosts the Bangsamoro Museum and has also served as a meeting place of the Parliament.
The regional seat is due to move to Parang in Maguindanao del Norte under Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 37, so this is the government as it sits now.
before_you_go: A working government compound. Expect a security check at the gate and bring identification.
Dress modestly, as for any public office in the region.
Ask before photographing buildings or staff inside the compound.
items.getting_there: In the BARMM Complex at Rosary Heights, Cotabato City.
items.best_time: Ramadhan, when the annual Ramadhan trade fair fills the centre with halal food, delicacies and crafts (in 2026 it opened on 16 February with 60 exhibitors).

do.title: See Toym Imao's Manara art installations

do.title: Look at the arcaded main building
do.detail: The 1976 central building, nicknamed the Little Malacañan of the South, is ringed by arcades with Muslim motifs on the roof; ask before photographing.

eat.title: Moro Cafe in the ORC compound
eat.detail: Moro Cafe is in the ORC compound on Gov. Gutierrez Avenue; Wikivoyage lists it open 8 am to 9 pm on weekdays and 7 am to 8 pm at weekends.

items.name: Rio Grande de Mindanao
items.summary: The second-largest river system in the Philippines, meeting the sea at Cotabato City.
detail: The Rio Grande de Mindanao drains about 23,169 square kilometres of central and eastern Mindanao, from the Pulangi headwaters in Bukidnon down to Illana Bay. Before it reaches the sea it splits into two arms, the Cotabato and the Tamontaka, separated by a hill.
It has always been the region's road. Farm produce still moves along it, Datu Piang and Cotabato City grew up on its banks, and in Cotabato houses line the riverfront.
The river is also where the Shariff Kabunsuan Festival holds its boat race and fluvial parade each December.
before_you_go: The riverside neighbourhoods are homes. Ask before photographing people or houses.
River trips are informal and arranged locally; there is no scheduled tour boat.
items.getting_there: The river runs through the city proper; the poblacion riverfront is the easiest place to see it.
items.best_time: December 15 to 19, when the Shariff Kabunsuan Festival holds its boat race on the river.

do.detail: The river wall in Cotabato City has been turned into a riverside park.

do.title: Watch the boat race at the Shariff Kabunsuan Festival
do.detail: The festival on December 15 to 19 includes a banca race and a re-enactment of Shariff Kabunsuan's arrival by river.

do.title: Arrange a boat trip on the river locally
do.detail: There is no scheduled tour boat; trips are informal and arranged with boat owners on the riverfront.

items.name: Bud Bongao
items.summary: A 314-meter peak above the capital, climbed as a pilgrimage and for the view.
detail: The mountain over Bongao is the province’s landmark and its most important site at once. Near the summit are graves held sacred by local Muslims, and people climb to visit them, to pray and to make vows — so the path carries pilgrims and sightseers on the same steps.

The climb takes roughly an hour to an hour and a half on a stepped and rooted trail through forest. Long-tailed macaques live on the mountain and gather along the route; climbers traditionally bring bananas for them.
The summit gives the whole archipelago — Sanga-Sanga, the reefs, and on a clear day the outer islands running south towards Borneo. It is the single best hour in BARMM.
before_you_go: This is a sacred site before it is a viewpoint. Dress modestly, keep your voice down near the graves, and follow what the people around you are doing.
Bring bananas for the macaques, and do not carry food loose or in an open bag — they will take it.
Start early. The trail is steep and unshaded in places and the heat builds fast.
Guides are available at the trailhead and are worth taking, both for the route and for what they can tell you about the site.
items.getting_there: The stepped trail of about 3,608 steps starts at the jump-off in Barangay Pasiagan, Bongao, and ends at a view deck on Tambisan Peak.
items.best_time: Early morning, before the heat builds (the guide's own advice).

do.title: Climb the stone steps to the view deck on Tambisan Peak
do.detail: A cobblestone trail of 3,608 steps runs from the jump-off at Barangay Pasiagan to a view deck at 317 metres, looking over the Celebes Sea to Tambisan Island in Sabah; start early, as the heat builds fast.

do.title: Register at the visitor centre before you climb
do.detail: In 2017 climbers registered and got a briefing at the visitor centre, and paid an entrance fee of PHP 20 towards upkeep.

do.title: Bring bananas for the macaques along the trail
do.detail: Friendly monkeys gather beside the path on the way up, so bring enough bananas for them, and keep other food in a closed bag.

do.title: Visit the tampat shrines near the summit, quietly and dressed modestly
do.detail: Pilgrims climb to pray at the burial shrines under the Tampat rocks, where 2 followers of Sheik Karimul Makhdum are said to be buried.

do.title: Look out from the peaks named after the islands they face
do.detail: The mountain has 6 limestone peaks, and each one looks out towards the island it is named after: Bongao, Simunul, Tambisan, Tinondakan, Pajar and Sibutu, the highest at 342 metres.

do.title: Tie a ribbon at the pagbaggut spots
do.detail: The registration office hands out coloured ribbons to tie near the summit while making a wish; each colour stands for a kind of wish, such as health, peace or success.

eat.title: A knickerbocker after the climb
eat.detail: Tawi-Tawi's knickerbocker, fruit in chilled cream topped with ice cream, is a common refreshment on a hot afternoon; a store at the jump-off sells snacks, drinks and bananas.

items.name: Panampangan Island
items.summary: A sandbar that runs for kilometers at low tide, and the clearest water in the region.
detail: Panampangan is a small island off Sapa-Sapa with a sandbar that, when the tide is out, extends into a strip of white sand running well over 3 kilometers out to sea. It is regularly described as the longest sandbar in the Philippines. Walking out along it, with water on both sides and no land ahead, is the reason people make the journey to Tawi-Tawi.
The water is exceptionally clear and the reef around the island is in good condition by national standards. Bring your own snorkel gear; nothing is rented here.
There is no resort, and only day trips are allowed now.
before_you_go: The sandbar exists at low tide. Check the tide table before you charter a boat, or you will arrive at open water.
Reached by boat from Bongao — a substantial crossing, chartered rather than scheduled. Arrange through the provincial tourism office or a Bongao operator.
Bring water, food, shade and everything else. There are no facilities.
Take your rubbish back with you; there is no collection.
items.getting_there: By chartered boat from Bongao; the island sits on Basibuli Shoal in Sapa-Sapa.
items.best_time: Low tide, when the sandbar is exposed.

do.title: Walk the sandbar at low tide
do.detail: The crescent-shaped sandbar runs out about 3,128 metres into Basibuli Shoal, so check the tide table before you charter the boat.

do.title: Picnic in the beach huts and grilling areas
do.detail: In 2018 there were huts and grilling areas on the beach for picnics, with Marines posted on the island; bring your own food, water and shade.

do.title: Swim and snorkel off the island
do.detail: The water is clear and the reef is in good condition, but nothing is rented here, so bring your own snorkel gear.

do.title: Stop at Simunul on the boat from Bongao
do.detail: The trip takes 30 minutes to 1 hour by speedboat or pump boat, and tours from Bongao often stop at Simunul for the Sheik Karimul Makhdum Mosque on the way.

do.title: Find the other 3 sandbars
do.detail: Besides the long one, the island has 3 more sandbars, 1 at the north-western end and 2 at the south-eastern end.

eat.title: Grilled reef fish under the coconut trees
eat.detail: Huts on the island serve Tausug dishes and freshly grilled fish; one group ate rabbitfish, unicornfish and barracuda. There is no drinking water on the island, so bring your own.

items.name: Sheik Karim al-Makhdum Mosque
items.summary: The site of the first mosque in the Philippines, founded in 1380.
detail: Sheik Karim al-Makhdum, an Arab missionary, reached Simunul in 1380 and built a mosque at Tubig Indangan. That is the beginning of Islam in the Philippines as a settled presence — roughly 140 years before Magellan landed at Cebu, and the fact that reorders most visitors’ sense of the country’s history.

The building has been replaced over the centuries, but four old hardwood pillars, which the National Museum dates to the 17th century, stand inside the present structure. Standing next to them is the whole visit. The site is a National Historical Landmark and the Sheik’s tomb is nearby.
before_you_go: Simunul is reached by boat from Bongao; there is no other way.
A working mosque and a pilgrimage site. Cover up, remove shoes, and ask before photographing the pillars or the tomb.
Coordinate through the municipality or the provincial tourism office rather than turning up.
items.getting_there: In Barangay Tubig Indangan on Simunul Island, reached by boat from Bongao.
items.best_time: Simunul marks the arrival of Sheikh Karimul Makhdum every November 7.

do.title: See the 4 old hardwood pillars inside the mosque
do.detail: The National Museum dated the pillars to the 17th century, which makes them the oldest known Islamic artefacts in the Philippines; ask before photographing them.

do.title: Visit Sheik Karimul Makhdum's tomb nearby
do.detail: The missionary's remains are buried close to the mosque; cover up and keep quiet, as at any pilgrimage site.

do.title: Come for Sheikh Karimul Makhdum Day on November 7
do.detail: Simunul marks the Sheik's arrival and the beginning of Islam in the country every November 7.

do.title: Swim at one of Simunul's beaches
do.detail: The municipality has 6 beaches across Simunul Island and Manuk Mangkaw Island, 3.5 km to the south.

do.title: Borrow proper clothes at the office beside the mosque
do.detail: The office next to the mosque lends visitors suitable attire for free; donations are welcome.

do.title: Swim at Bohe Sallang
do.detail: Bohe Sallang is a small public freshwater lagoon on Simunul, cold and deep, where locals dive and swim at weekends.

do.title: Catch the noon boat and stay the night
do.detail: Public boats to Simunul usually leave the Chinese Pier in Bongao around noon and the return boat leaves at about 8 am, so without a chartered boat you stay overnight.

items.name: Sitangkai
items.summary: A town built over open water, where the streets are boardwalks and boats.
detail: Sitangkai is the southernmost town in the Philippines and it is built on stilts over the shallows, with plank walkways instead of roads and boats instead of tricycles. It is a Sama Dilaut town, and the relationship with the sea here is not scenic — it is the entire structure of daily life.
Seaweed is the economy. The racks, the drying lines and the sorting go on everywhere, and the smell and the rhythm of it is the town.
It is a long way from anywhere and the journey is a large part of what you are signing up for.
before_you_go: Reached by boat from Bongao via Sibutu; count on the better part of a day each way.
People live here and their houses are what you would be photographing. Ask, every time.
Coordinate with the municipality. Arriving unannounced in a small town at the end of the country reads badly.
items.getting_there: By boat from Bongao via Sibutu.
items.best_time: A weekend, when traders barter and sell at the market along the town's canals; public boats from Bongao leave on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.

do.title: Get around town by boat and plank footbridge
do.detail: Boats are the main way to get around and footbridges link one house to the next, which is why the town is called the Venice of the South.

do.title: Watch the seaweed being dried and sorted
do.detail: Seaweed racks, drying lines and sorting are everywhere in town; ask before photographing people and their houses.

do.title: Plan the trip with the municipality
do.detail: Count on most of a day each way by boat from Bongao via Sibutu, and let the municipality know before you arrive.

do.title: Browse the canal market by boat
do.detail: Market vendors line the wide main canal, which serves as the town's high street.

do.title: Take the Monday, Wednesday or Friday ferry from Bongao
do.detail: A 2026 listing gives Wita Ferries trips from Bongao to Sitangkai via Sibutu on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, about 1 hour 45 minutes; an older account describes a slower passenger boat from Bongao Port taking 5 to 6 hours.

items.name: Turtle Islands
items.summary: Green sea turtle nesting beaches, protected jointly with Malaysia.
detail: A cluster of islands west of Tawi-Tawi proper that form one of the most significant green sea turtle nesting grounds in Southeast Asia. Baguan is the main sanctuary island, and the whole group is managed as a transboundary protected area shared with Malaysia — the only arrangement of its kind in the region.
Nesting happens year-round with seasonal peaks, and seeing it is a matter of being on the right beach at night with the people who are permitted to be there.

The Turtle Islands Wildlife Sanctuary, a protected area since 1999, covers 242,967 hectares of sea and the islands of Baguan, Taganak, Boan, Great Bakkungan, Langaan and Lihiman; all are inhabited except Baguan. It averages more than 13,000 turtle nests a year, is an ASEAN Heritage Park and is on UNESCO's tentative World Heritage list. From Bongao the only way there is by sea, a trip of 15 to 16 hours.
before_you_go: This is a protected area, not an attraction. Access requires clearance and is arranged through the protected-area management and the municipality — not on arrival.
The crossing is long and weather-dependent.
No lights, no flash, no handling. The rules exist because the turtles abandon nesting attempts.
items.getting_there: There is no regular transport to the islands; access to the sanctuary zones is only with the supervision of government staff.
items.best_time: Night, when the turtles come ashore to lay their eggs; the boardwalks and watching lounges planned for Taganak, Bakkungan and Baguan were designed for night viewing.

do.title: Watch the turtles nest at night, with supervision
do.detail: Visitors come to watch green turtles lay their eggs at night, and outside the strict protection zones visits are allowed only with guidance from government staff; no lights, flash or handling.

do.title: Go between late August and December
do.detail: From the end of August to December the turtles come ashore by the hundreds to lay their eggs.

do.title: Watch the hatchlings head for the sea
do.detail: Visitors to Baguan, the main sanctuary island, also come to watch hatchlings climb out of their nests and make for the water.

do.title: Look for the islands' birds
do.detail: At least 71 bird species have been recorded, among them the Philippine megapode, the grey imperial pigeon and the Mantanani scops owl.

items.name: Balobok Rock Shelter
items.summary: A cave on Sanga-Sanga that holds some of the oldest evidence of people in Southeast Asia.
detail: The rock shelter at Lakit-Lakit, on Sanga-Sanga island in Bongao, housed one of the oldest human settlements in Southeast Asia, dated to between 8,000 and 5,000 years ago. Bones, jars, shells and other artifacts have been recovered from it.

It was recognized as an Important Cultural Property in 2016, and a bill filed in the Bangsamoro Parliament in 2022 proposed recognizing the area as a regional heritage zone. In the 1970s the cave served as a shelter for the Moro National Liberation Front.
There is nothing built for visitors here. The interest is in standing where people lived thousands of years before anything else in this guide existed.
before_you_go: An archaeological site: touch nothing and take nothing.
Arrange a visit through the municipality or the provincial tourism office rather than looking for it alone.
items.getting_there: In Barangay Lakit-Lakit on Sanga-Sanga, the island north of Bongao that also holds the province's airport.

do.title: Visit the shelter with the municipality or tourism office
do.detail: People lived in this cave between 8,000 and 5,000 years ago; nothing is built for visitors, so arrange a visit and touch nothing.

do.title: Watch wooden boats being built on Sanga-Sanga
do.detail: Large wooden prahu boats are built by hand around Sanga-Sanga, mostly by Sama-Bajau craftsmen, and each one takes about a year.

do.title: Watch the cliff divers at Lakit-Lakit
do.detail: Guides pair the cave with a nearby spot in Lakit-Lakit where locals go cliff diving.

do.title: Stop at Yanas Farm for the view
do.detail: A 2022 itinerary stopped at Yanas Farm in Lakit-Lakit for its sunset view, paying PHP 50 each.

items.name: Sibutu Island
items.summary: A large low island near the Sabah border, home to boat builders and an important site for nature conservation.
detail: Sibutu covers about 109 square kilometres and lies some 14 kilometres from the coast of Sabah. Its people are mostly boat builders, and they also trade seaweed, firewood and stone.
Four small uninhabited islands lie 3.5 to 6 kilometres south of it, ending at Saluag, the southernmost island of the Philippines. The island is counted as an important site for nature conservation.

Through an error in the Treaty of Paris, Sibutu and Cagayan de Sulu stayed under Spain after the rest of the country passed to the United States, until the Treaty of Washington was ratified in 1901. It is also the waypoint on the long boat journey from Bongao to Sitangkai.
before_you_go: Reached by boat from Bongao; plan for a long crossing.
Coordinate with the municipality before arriving.
items.getting_there: By boat from Bongao; it is the stop before Sitangkai on the route south.

do.title: Watch boat builders at work
do.detail: Most people on Sibutu build boats, and a wooden prahu built entirely by hand takes about a year.

do.title: Break the boat journey from Bongao to Sitangkai here
do.detail: Sibutu is the stop on the long crossing to Sitangkai; let the municipality know before you arrive.

do.title: Look for the carved wooden grave markers
do.detail: Woodcarving is common on Sibutu, and ornate wooden markers are a frequent sight.

do.title: Go on to Saluag, the southernmost island
do.detail: From Tandu Banak or Sibutu town, take a habal-habal to Tandu Owak and charter a boat for the 30-minute crossing to Saluag, which has an old and a new lighthouse.

items.name: Panguan Island
items.summary: A white-sand islet at the very edge of the country, the last island of the Sulu Archipelago before Malaysia.
detail: Panguan is a tiny island of about 0.06 square kilometres in Sitangkai, 50 kilometres from Sabah. Its other name, Malamanok, means eat chicken in Sama-Bajau: travellers heading to Sabah stopped here to eat roasted chicken before the last leg.

A small Sama Dilaut community lives here alongside a military barrack and a flagpole. The island was used as a hideout by the Abu Sayyaf until Philippine Marines took it in April 2017, and the flag went up on 29 April that year.
The provincial tourism office counts it among Tawi-Tawi's most visited spots.
before_you_go: A border island with a military presence. Go only with the municipality's and the provincial tourism office's clearance.
Like other border communities it lacks food, drinking water and health care; bring everything you need and leave nothing behind.
items.getting_there: By boat via Sitangkai, near the Philippine-Malaysian border.

do.title: See the flagpole at the edge of the country
do.detail: The Philippine flag was raised here on 29 April 2017, beside a military barrack, on the last island of the Sulu Archipelago before Malaysia, 50 km from Sabah.

do.title: Go only with clearance and bring everything
do.detail: Clear the trip with the municipality and the provincial tourism office, and bring your own food and drinking water, since the island has little of either.

items.name: Lake Lanao
items.summary: The second-largest lake in the country, and one of a handful of ancient lakes in the world.
detail: Lake Lanao fills a highland basin at around 700 meters and covers some 340 square kilometers. It is old — old enough that its fish evolved into species found nowhere else, which is the technical sense in which it is called an ancient lake, and several of those species are now in serious trouble.

It drains through the Agus River to Maria Cristina Falls at Iligan, which is why a lake in Lanao del Sur has historically supplied a large share of Mindanao’s electricity. The lake level and the power system are politically entangled and locally contentious.

For a visitor, the lake is a circuit rather than a viewpoint: the road runs around the shore through Marantao, Tugaya, Bacolod-Kalawi, Ganassi and Binidayan, and the towns are the reason to drive it. Late afternoon light over the water from the western shore is the shot everyone comes back with.
before_you_go: A hired vehicle with a local driver is the practical way to do the circuit. Public transport works but eats the day.
It is genuinely cool at altitude, especially after dark. Bring a layer.
Ask locally about current conditions on the southern shore before committing to the full loop.
items.getting_there: Marawi on the northern shore is the base. Jeepneys and vans leave the South Bound terminal in Iligan for Marawi, and UV Express minivans run often; the nearest airport with flights is Laguindingan, between Cagayan de Oro and Iligan.
items.best_time: December to April are the least rainy months at Marawi (about 140 to 185 mm a month) and May to July the wettest (330 to 415 mm); it is cool all year, with highs of 24 to 26°C. July brings the month-long Lanao del Sur founding anniversary.

do.detail: Hire a vehicle with a local driver for the loop through Marantao, Tugaya, Bacolod-Kalawi, Ganassi and Binidayan, and ask about the southern shore before doing the full circuit.

do.title: Look over the lake from Angoyao Hills
do.detail: Angoyao Hills in Barangay Sogod, Marawi, is a natural viewpoint over the lake.

do.title: Go down to Bagang beach
do.detail: Bagang beach is 2 km from Marawi's commercial centre.

do.title: Visit the Polo Barakat Mosque in Binidayan
do.detail: The provincial tourism office lists this mosque in Binidayan, on the lake circuit, among the province's draws; dress modestly.

eat.title: Maranao sweets and snacks
eat.detail: Maranao foods to look for in Lanao del Sur include amik, dodol, browa, tiyateg, tamongkosi, barobed, soman and apang.

items.name: Aga Khan Museum of Islamic Arts
items.summary: The best collection of Maranao and Mindanao material anywhere, on the MSU campus.
detail: Inside Mindanao State University in Marawi, and the single most rewarding indoor hour in BARMM. The collection covers Maranao brass and okir carving, kulintang instruments, textiles, weaponry and torogan architectural elements — panolong beam ends carved into the winged forms that are the signature of the tradition.
It is a university museum rather than a national one, which means the labeling can be uneven and the presentation is plain. The objects carry it.
before_you_go: On a university campus; entry is through MSU. Confirm it is open before traveling, as hours have varied.
Photography rules vary by gallery — ask at the desk.
items.getting_there: Inside the Mindanao State University campus in Marawi. From Iligan's South Bound terminal take a jeepney or van to Marawi, then a tricycle; ask for MSU if the driver does not know the museum.
items.best_time: A weekday: a visitor who came on a Sunday found it closed.

do.title: See the weapons from the Moro wars
do.detail: The museum shows weapons used against the Spanish and the Americans, including the lantaka cannon, the kris and the kampilan.

do.title: See the model pagoda mosques and torogan parts
do.detail: Miniature pagoda-style mosques, replicas and pieces of torogan houses such as the carved panolong beam ends are on display, along with musical instruments and farm tools.

do.title: Find Abdulmari Imao's calligraphic sculptures
do.detail: In 2016 the museum was reported to hold more than 300 of Abdulmari Imao's calligraphic sculptures of the name of Allah.

do.title: Go up to the natural history floor
do.detail: The second floor holds the natural history collection and some traditional costumes, and the museum also has old photographs of Marawi from the American period.

do.title: Take a tricycle to MSU and check it is open
do.detail: Tricycles are the easiest way to get around Marawi, so ask for MSU if the driver does not know the museum; hours have varied, so confirm before you travel and ask at the desk about photography.

eat.title: Snacks at JECOs Cafe
eat.detail: JECOs, at the MCU Commercial Center, is among the best-known places to eat in the city, serving snacks and desserts from 10 am to 8 pm.

items.name: Tugaya
items.summary: The brass and craft town of the Maranao, on the western shore of the lake.
detail: Tugaya is where Maranao brass is made — kulintang gong sets, gadur vessels, betel boxes, and the cast and engraved work that carries okir ornament. It is a working craft town rather than a market: the casting, the engraving and the finishing happen in the houses and workshops along the road.
Woodcarving and weaving are here too, and the town is the practical answer to the question of where the objects in the Aga Khan Museum come from.
Buying directly from a workshop is normal and is the point of coming. Brass is heavy — plan for that before you fall in love with a gadur.
before_you_go: Ask before photographing inside a workshop; it is someone’s livelihood and their technique.
Prices are negotiated. Bring cash — nothing here takes a card.
Combine it with the lake circuit rather than making it a separate trip.
items.best_time: December to April, the least rainy months on the lake; May to July are the wettest.

do.detail: Tugaya's foundries cast brass and bronze by the lost-wax method, including the gador, a pair of ornate brass urns; ask before photographing inside a workshop.

do.detail: Buying direct is the point of coming: prices are negotiated, nothing takes a card, so bring cash, and remember that brass is heavy.

do.title: See the langkit panels woven for the malong landap
do.detail: Weavers here use back-strap looms and slow needle-weaving to make langkit panels, which are sewn into the traditional Maranao malong landap.

do.title: See okir chests inlaid with shell
do.detail: Workshops under the houses make gongs, drums and baul, wooden chests carved with okir and inlaid with polished tipay shell.

items.name: Kawayan Torogan
items.summary: A declared National Cultural Treasure, and the last torogan of its kind.
detail: The torogan is the Maranao royal house: a raised timber hall on massive posts, with the panolong — the carved beam ends that project from the facade like wings — as its defining feature. It was a datu’s residence and the seat of his authority, and very few survive.

The Kawayan Torogan at Marantao, built for Sultan sa Kawayan, is a declared National Cultural Treasure and the most intact example left. Its condition has been a long-running concern and restoration has been intermittent.
Seeing one standing, rather than a panolong in a museum case, changes how the ornament reads. The carving is architecture, not decoration.
before_you_go: Privately connected to the family that holds it. Arrange a visit locally rather than turning up.
Condition varies and parts may not be enterable.

do.title: Arrange a visit with the family that holds the house
do.detail: The house is privately connected to the family that holds it, so arrange your visit locally, and expect that parts of it may be closed.

do.title: Look at the carved panolong beam ends
do.detail: The butterfly-shaped beam ends are carved in turn with the naga (serpent) and the pako rabong (growing fern), the classic Maranao okir motifs.

do.title: See the posts set on boulders
do.detail: The house stands on huge tree-trunk posts resting on rounded boulders, so that it can move without falling in an earthquake and is protected from rot and termites.

items.name: Marawi’s Most Affected Area
items.summary: The city center destroyed in the 2017 siege, and the slow work of rebuilding it.
detail: For five months in 2017 the center of Marawi was fought over street by street, and at the end of it the commercial and residential core of the city was rubble. Around 200,000 people were displaced. The area is officially the Most Affected Area and universally called Ground Zero.
Rebuilding has been slow, contested, and is still incomplete. Some residents have returned, many have not, and the question of compensation remains live. Mosques stand roofless in the middle of it.

Visitors do come, and people here will generally talk about what happened. But the distinction between witnessing and sightseeing matters enormously in a place where the person you are talking to lost their house, and possibly more.
before_you_go: Go with a local contact. This is not a place to wander into alone with a camera.
Ask before photographing anything, and accept no as an answer.
Sections remain restricted or unsafe. Follow what you are told on the ground.
If you buy nothing else on your trip, buy your lunch here.
items.getting_there: By tricycle from the city across a new bridge into the area; public access was allowed again in 2022 after explosives and debris were cleared, and the rebuilt roads here continue towards Bukidnon. A 2022 visit with a resident took about 3 hours.

items.name: Marawi Grand Mosque
items.summary: Marawi's great mosque, damaged in the 2017 siege and rebuilt by 2021 to hold 20,000 worshippers.
detail: The mosque in Pangarungan Village was begun in the 1950s and finished in 1970, led by the landowner Datu Pangarungan Disalongan with money from local families and foreign donors. Visiting ministers from the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation often stopped here.
Militants captured it during the 2017 siege, and it was left heavily damaged. Repairs finished in October 2021 and the building was handed over to the mosque's president and chairman that December.
The rebuilt mosque has three floors and a basement over 9,434 square metres, with room for 20,000 worshippers, which makes it the biggest Islamic place of worship in the Philippines.
before_you_go: A working mosque: dress covered, women bring a headscarf, and shoes come off before the prayer hall.
Avoid Friday midday prayer unless you are attending.
Ask before photographing people, and never photograph anyone praying.
items.getting_there: On Disalongan Street in Pangarungan Village, Marawi City.

items.name: Lake Dapao
items.summary: A deep lake south-west of Lake Lanao, up to 120 metres deep and protected as a national park since 1965.
detail: Lake Dapao covers about 10 square kilometres in Pualas and reaches a maximum depth of 120 metres, which puts it among the deepest lakes in the country. It is fed by run-off and several small rivers.

It was declared a national park in 1965 under Republic Act 4190. Snakehead, tilapia, carp, goby and catfish live in it; the endangered Barbodes tumba once did, but none were found in 1982 fieldwork and it is thought to be locally extinct.
before_you_go: There are no visitor facilities; go with a local contact from Pualas.
Boats on the lake belong to fishing families. Ask, and pay, if you want to go out on the water.
items.getting_there: In the municipality of Pualas, south-west of Lake Lanao.

do.title: Go out on the lake with a fishing family
do.detail: The boats belong to fishing families, so ask before going out on the water, and pay.

do.title: Visit with a local contact from Pualas
do.detail: There are no visitor facilities at the lake.

items.name: Lake Butig
items.summary: A small forest lake at 500 metres in the southern highlands, with Mount Makaturing as its backdrop.
detail: Lake Butig lies at the foot of the Butig mountains in Barangay Pindolonan, about 500 metres above sea level. It and its surrounding forest make up a 68-hectare national park declared in 1965.

The cool climate draws visitors and a swimming resort has been set up on the shore. Hornbills, parrots, woodpeckers and wild ducks live in the forest, along with Philippine monkeys, deer and wild pigs.
Mount Makaturing, a 1,940-metre volcano, rises behind it.
before_you_go: Butig is well off the usual circuit. Get current local advice before setting out, and go with a contact from the area.
items.getting_there: About 30 km from Marawi via the Lake Lanao Circumferential Road.

do.title: Swim at the lakeshore resort
do.detail: The lake sits at 500 metres and a swimming resort has been set up on the shore for people who come to cool off.

do.title: Look for hornbills and wild ducks in the forest
do.detail: The 68-hectare park's forest has hornbills, parrots, woodpeckers and wild ducks, as well as monkeys, deer and wild pigs.

do.title: Drive in on the Lake Lanao Circumferential Road
do.detail: The lake is about 30 km from Marawi by the circumferential road; get current local advice before setting out.

items.name: Sacred Mountain National Park
items.summary: A 94-hectare national park on the edge of Marawi, built around a 274-metre extinct volcanic cone with a pond on top.
detail: The park spans Barangays Guimba and Papandayan and was established in 1965. Its main feature is Mount Mupo, an extinct volcanic cone 274 metres high, and the trek to the summit ends at a pond.
It is a place for birdwatching and walking. Buyo-buyo plants dominate the slopes, alongside introduced African tulip trees.
The name was given by the national government in the 1960s in place of the mountain's own local name, and some residents have asked for it to be renamed to reflect that.
before_you_go: Take a local guide for the trek; there is no marked visitor trail.
Early morning for birds.
items.getting_there: In Barangays Guimba and Papandayan, Marawi City.
items.best_time: December to April are the least rainy months at Marawi (about 140 to 185 mm a month) and May to July the wettest (330 to 415 mm); it is cool all year, with highs of 24 to 26°C.

do.title: Trek to the pond at the top of Mount Mupo
do.detail: The trail up the 274-metre extinct volcanic cone ends at a pond at the summit; there is no marked trail, so take a local guide.

do.title: Go birdwatching in the early morning
do.detail: The park is known for birdwatching, and early morning is the best time.

items.name: The Upi uplands
items.summary: Cool highland country, and the heartland of the Teduray.
detail: The road climbs out of the coastal plain into Upi and South Upi and the temperature drops with it. This is Teduray country — one of the region’s indigenous non-Muslim peoples — and the landscape of rolling upland farms is unlike anywhere else in the province.
The Meguyaya Festival is the moment the culture is most visible: Teduray dress, music, and the agricultural thanksgiving the festival is built around.
It is also simply a good drive, with views back down over the plain towards Cotabato City.
before_you_go: The last stretches are rough after heavy rain; a high-clearance vehicle helps.
Cooler than the coast, especially in the early morning.
items.best_time: December, for the weeks-long Mëguyaya Festival; the 23rd edition ended on 22 December 2025 with a street-dance parade, after a tri-people thanksgiving feast and the Maisan Na! corn feast.

images.author: LuzViMindaLife
images.caption: Rice fields and mountains in the upland town of Upi

do.title: Go for the Meguyaya Festival in December
do.detail: Meguyaya, the Teduray harvest thanksgiving, is held every December with street dancing that shows the Teduray, Maguindanaon and settler cultures, cultural nights and a trade fair.

do.title: Drive up from the coastal plain
do.detail: The road climbs into cool farm country with views back over the plain towards Cotabato City; the last stretches are rough after rain, so a high-clearance vehicle helps.

eat.title: Roast corn at the Maisan Na grills
eat.detail: During Meguyaya a long line of grills is set up beside the road, where everyone roasts corn together.

items.name: The Illana Bay coast
items.summary: Beaches, small islands and the region’s deepwater port, north-west of the city.
detail: Parang faces Illana Bay and is the closest stretch of proper coast to Cotabato City — beaches, offshore islets, and the fishing economy that goes with them. Polloc port here is the region’s deepwater harbour and the site of its freeport, so the working coast and the swimming coast sit side by side.
Bongo Island lies off the mouth of the bay and is reachable by boat from the mainland.
This is where people from the city go at the weekend, which is the most honest recommendation available.
before_you_go: Facilities are basic and vary by beach. Bring what you need.
Boats to the islands are arranged at the shore and negotiated.
Swimwear norms here are local norms — most people swim covered.
items.getting_there: By road on the Narciso Ramos Highway, part of the Pan-Philippine Highway, which links Parang with its neighbouring towns.
items.best_time: December to April, the driest months (about 40 to 55 mm of rain a month); June to August are the wettest. The town festival is on August 18.

do.title: Swim at Zone Beach or Punta Beach
do.detail: These are 2 of the beaches Parang lists among its attractions; facilities are basic and most people swim covered.

do.title: Take a boat across to Bongo Island
do.detail: Boats to the islands are arranged at the shore and the price is negotiated.

do.title: Visit the fruit bat sanctuary
do.detail: Parang lists a fruit bat sanctuary among its attractions.

do.title: Come for Parang's founding day on August 18
do.detail: The town holds a cultural festival every August 18, its founding anniversary.

items.name: Mount Minandar
items.summary: A grass-covered mountain near Cotabato City, about a two-hour hike to the summit.
detail: Mount Minandar rises in Barangay Kusiong and is known for its green colour, because it is covered mostly in grass rather than forest.
The climb from the foot to the summit takes about two hours, which makes it the closest proper hike to Cotabato City.
Kusiong also has the town's beaches, so a climb and a swim fit in the same day.
before_you_go: Go with a local guide arranged in Kusiong.
There is little shade on a grass mountain; start early and carry water.
items.getting_there: The climb starts in Barangay Kusiong, Datu Odin Sinsuat.
items.best_time: December to April are the driest months (about 20 to 30 mm of rain a month), June to August the wettest.

do.title: Hike 2 hours to the grassy summit
do.detail: The climb from the foot to the summit takes about 2 hours; there is little shade, so start early, carry water and arrange a guide in Kusiong.

do.title: Finish with a swim at Kusiong Beach
do.detail: The town's beaches are in the same barangay, so a climb and a swim fit into one day.

items.name: The Blue Lagoon
items.summary: A deep, spring-fed pool of bright blue water in the forest, a few steps off the highway.
detail: The lagoon in Barangay Margues is the town's top tourist attraction: a small pool of startlingly blue spring water, a few steps from the main road, whose bottom no one has reached. Older residents say enchantresses live in it, which is where the other name comes from.

It is not developed. The water flows on into a stream and then the Tamontaka River, and the village has no other source of drinking water, so people fetch water here early in the morning and late in the evening and wash and bathe here too.
A second blue lagoon lies in neighbouring Bitu, 100 stone steps below the highway and a 15 to 20 minute walk away.
before_you_go: This is the village's drinking water. No soap, no sunscreen, no rubbish, and give way to people fetching water.
Swimmers jump into deep water here; it is unguarded.
items.getting_there: From Awang in Cotabato City take a multicab bound for Isulan and get off at Margues Elementary School; the lagoon is a few steps from the road.
items.best_time: Morning, when the water looks bluest.

images.caption: The blue spring-fed lagoon in the forest at Datu Odin Sinsuat

do.title: Swim, or jump into the deep blue water
do.detail: Local teenagers dive into the lagoon from above; it is deep and unguarded, so no soap, no sunscreen, and give way to people fetching water.

do.title: Come in the morning, when the water is bluest
do.detail: The lagoon looks bluest in the morning, but villagers fetch drinking water here early in the morning and late in the evening, so keep out of their way.

do.detail: From Cotabato City, take a multicab bound for Isulan at Awang and get off at Margues Elementary School (the fare was PHP 10 in 2015); the lagoon is a few steps from the road.

do.title: Walk on to the second lagoon at Bitu
do.detail: The Bitu lagoon is 100 stone steps down from the highway and a 15 to 20 minute walk from Margues.

items.name: Kusiong Beach
items.summary: A grey-sand beach lined with resorts, and the nearest beach to Cotabato City.
detail: Kusiong is a stretch of greyish sand on the coast of Datu Odin Sinsuat with a run of small resorts, among them Amaya, Sahara and Precious Cabana.
It is the closest beach to Cotabato City.
Mount Minandar is in the same barangay.
before_you_go: Entry is through the resorts; ask about their rules on arrival.
Most people swim covered here.
items.getting_there: In Barangay Kusiong, Datu Odin Sinsuat, the nearest beach to Cotabato City.
items.best_time: December to April are the driest months (about 20 to 30 mm of rain a month), June to August the wettest.

do.title: Swim from one of the beach resorts
do.detail: You get onto the beach through resorts such as Amaya, Sahara and Precious Cabana; ask about their rules when you arrive.

do.title: Climb Mount Minandar in the same barangay
do.detail: The grassy mountain is about a 2-hour hike to the summit from its foot in Kusiong.

items.name: Masjid Datu Untong Balabaran
items.summary: A tiered, pagoda-style mosque in Taviran, one of the last of its kind in the Philippines.
detail: Before the domed Arabian style arrived with pilgrims returning from Mecca, mosques in the Philippines were built as tiered, pagoda-like halls of three, five or eight levels. Very few survive, and the form is now considered endangered.

The mosque of Datu Untong Balabaran in Barangay Taviran is named as one of the last standing examples in Mindanao. Seeing it is the clearest way to understand what the first mosque at Simunul probably looked like.
It has been proposed, with other heritage mosques, for the Philippines' tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage status.
before_you_go: A working mosque: dress covered, shoes off, and a headscarf for women.
Ask permission before going in or taking photographs.
items.getting_there: In Barangay Taviran, Datu Odin Sinsuat.

images.author: Marwan Khan
images.caption: The white Taviran mosque with its tiered roof, on a grassy rise among palms.

do.title: Ask to see the tiered pagoda-style mosque
do.detail: It is one of the last pagoda-style mosques still standing in the Philippines; ask permission before going in or taking photographs, and dress covered.

do.title: Picture the first mosque at Simunul
do.detail: The first mosque at Simunul was probably built in this same pagoda style, so this is the closest you can get to seeing what it looked like.

items.name: Bongo Island
items.summary: The province's one offshore island, at the mouth of Illana Bay, with a white-sand beach at Limbayan.
detail: Bongo is the outlying island of Maguindanao del Norte, under the municipality of Parang. Parang lists the white-sand beach at Limbayan on Bongo Island among its attractions.
It is the island the guide's Illana Bay entry points to, and the reason to cross from the mainland.
before_you_go: Boats are arranged at the Parang shore and negotiated.
Facilities are basic. Bring water and food.
items.getting_there: By boat from the Parang mainland.
items.best_time: December to April, the driest months on this coast; June to August are the wettest.

images.author: Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources and Energy (BARMM)
images.caption: An aerial view of a shoreline village on Bongo Island, backed by coconut groves and a wide tidal flat.

do.title: Swim at the white-sand beach at Limbayan
do.detail: Parang lists the white-sand beach at Limbayan on Bongo Island among its attractions; bring water and food.

do.title: Hire a boat across from the Parang shore
do.detail: Boats are arranged on the Parang shore and the price is negotiated.

items.name: Masjid Dimaukom
items.summary: A mosque painted entirely pink, built by Muslim and Christian hands together.
detail: It is exactly as photographed: a mosque, domes and minarets and walls, in an unbroken pink. It was built at the initiative of the town’s then-mayor, and the story attached to it — that the color stands for peace and love, and that Muslim and Christian workers built it side by side in a province better known for the opposite — is the reason it traveled beyond the region.

The temptation is to treat it as a photo stop, and most visitors do. It is worth staying long enough to notice that it is an ordinary working mosque in an ordinary Maguindanaon town, which is rather the point being made.
before_you_go: A working mosque: cover up, shoes off inside, and a scarf for women in the prayer hall.
Reached from Cotabato City by bus on the General Santos highway; ask locally about the road and the current situation before setting out.
Do not treat the interior as a photo set. Ask.
items.getting_there: On the Cotabato City–General Santos highway, about 42 km from Cotabato City. Take a Husky bus bound for General Santos (50 minutes to an hour, PHP 105 to 150 in 2018) and get off at the Datu Saudi Ampatuan municipal hall; the mosque is a few metres from the pink rotunda. From General Santos it is about 3 hours.
items.best_time: Early morning: a visitor at 8 am found it almost empty.

images.author: Patrickroque01
images.caption: Masjid Dimaukom, the Pink Mosque, on the Salbu-Pagatin road in Datu Saudi Ampatuan

do.title: Visit the mosque, dressed covered
do.detail: It is a working mosque: cover up, take your shoes off inside, women wear a scarf in the prayer hall, and ask before photographing the interior.

do.title: Look for the town's other pink buildings
do.detail: The mayor who built the mosque also had other buildings in Datu Saudi Ampatuan painted pink, including the municipal hall.

do.title: Register at the gate
do.detail: There is no entrance fee; visitors sign in at the gate, where tips are welcome.

items.name: Ligawasan Marsh
items.summary: One of the largest wetlands in the country — channels, floating vegetation, birds.
detail: The marsh spreads across the Maguindanao lowlands where the Rio Grande de Mindanao slows and spreads, and it is enormous — a shifting system of open water, channels and floating mats that changes shape between wet and dry season. It is one of the country’s most important wetlands for birds, and a fishery that a great many families live from.
It also sits on substantial natural gas reserves, which has made it a subject of regional politics for decades and is part of why it has never been developed for visitors.
Seeing it means getting in a boat with someone who knows the channels. There is no other version of this trip.
before_you_go: A boat and a local guide, arranged in the barangay. Nothing is scheduled or ticketed.
Fuller and more navigable in the wet season; easier to reach by road in the dry.
This area needs current local advice before you travel. Ask, and take the answer seriously.
Early morning for birds, as everywhere.
items.getting_there: Nothing is scheduled. A 2019 birdwatching trip organised with the mayor of General S.K. Pendatun set off by canoe before dawn, escorted by the army and police.
items.best_time: Dawn, for the birds; the 2019 birding trip was over by 9:30 am. In the dry season up to 140,000 hectares more land emerges from the water.

images.author: Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit, Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center
images.caption: The Liguasan Marsh seen from the International Space Station in 2013, the Mindanao River meandering through its wetlands.

do.title: Take a boat through the channels with a local guide
do.detail: Arrange the boat and guide in the barangay; nothing is scheduled, and the marsh is easier to get around by boat in the wet season.

do.title: See the water lilies turn the marsh pink
do.detail: When the water lilies bloom, parts of the marsh turn into a sea of pink.

do.title: Look for the comb-crested jacana at dawn
do.detail: The marsh is the only place in the Philippines where the comb-crested jacana can be seen, among at least 92 bird species recorded here.

eat.title: Tapul rice from the marsh farms
eat.detail: The marsh's farmland grows prized rice varieties called tapul or denorado; tilapia and mudfish are raised in its waters.

items.name: Lake Buluan
items.summary: The third-largest lake in Mindanao, a wide shallow basin ringed by mountains.
detail: Lake Buluan covers about 61 square kilometres and sits just 4.5 metres above sea level. It is shared between Buluan and Mangudadatu in Maguindanao del Sur and two towns of Sultan Kudarat province.

It is a basin of linked marshes where the Pulangi, Maanoy, Buluan and Alah rivers gather on their way to the Mindanao River, and it was once ringed by the Sultanate of Buayan. Snakehead, catfish, carp, milkfish and tilapia are fished here.
Mining in the neighbouring provinces is named as a threat to the lake.

The lake spans more than 6,000 hectares, about 70% of it shared between Buluan and Mangudadatu. Fish-pen farming of tilapia has grown here with fingerlings, boats and cages from the regional agriculture ministry, and fishers read the water's colour: green is good for the fish, reddish or very clear warns of bad weather.
before_you_go: Go out on the water only with a local boatman.
Ask locally about current conditions before travelling.
items.getting_there: On the edge of Buluan town, the provincial capital.
items.best_time: Sunrise, when fishers paddle out to their nets and tilapia pens; December to April are the driest months.

do.title: Go out on the lake with a local boatman
do.detail: Fishers here catch snakehead, catfish, carp, milkfish and tilapia; go out only with a boatman, and ask about current conditions first.

do.title: Watch the tilapia pens being fed
do.detail: Fishers keep tilapia in pens on the lake, one of them more than a hectare; fingerlings are fed 3 times a day in fine-mesh nets before moving to larger pens.

eat.title: Buluan Lake tilapia
eat.detail: Tilapia from the lake's pens is sold as far as Davao, Pagadian and Cotabato City.

items.name: Maliga Walay
items.summary: The historic red house of Datu Piang, now the town's municipal building.
detail: Maliga Walay means red house. It is a historic building associated with Datu Piang and the history of Maguindanao, and it now serves as the municipal building of the town that carries his name.
Datu Piang sits on the Rio Grande de Mindanao and is also one of the towns where Inaul weaving, the Maguindanaon handwoven textile, is still practised.
before_you_go: A working government building; ask at the municipal office before looking around.
items.getting_there: In the town of Datu Piang, on the Rio Grande de Mindanao.

images.author: Provincial Government of Maguindanao del Sur
images.caption: The red two-storey Maliga Walay, now the municipal hall of Datu Piang.

do.title: See the red house, now the town hall
do.detail: The historic house of Datu Piang now serves as the municipal building, so ask at the municipal office before looking around.

do.title: Watch inaul being woven in Datu Piang
do.detail: Datu Piang is one of the towns where the Maguindanaon handwoven inaul is still made, and visitors can watch it being woven and buy it.

items.name: Kuhan Falls
items.summary: A cascading waterfall in the mountains of South Upi, in Teduray country.
detail: Kuhan Falls is a series of cascades in a lush, mountainous part of South Upi.
South Upi is also where Monom, the Teduray weaving and craft tradition, is practised; visitors can watch the artisans work and buy from them directly.
before_you_go: Go with a local guide arranged in South Upi.
Buy crafts from the makers; that is how the trip helps the town.

images.author: Provincial Government of Maguindanao del Sur
images.caption: Kuhan Falls pours down a forested cliff into a pool in South Upi.

do.title: Walk to the cascades with a local guide
do.detail: The falls run down in a series of cascades through lush mountain country; arrange a guide in South Upi.

do.title: Watch Teduray Monom weavers and buy from them
do.detail: In South Upi visitors can watch the Monom weaving and craft work and buy directly from the artisans.

items.name: Lamitan City
items.summary: Basilan’s BARMM capital, and the center of Yakan life.
detail: Lamitan is the most approachable part of Basilan and the place a first visit is built around. It is the provincial capital for BARMM purposes, it has the market where Yakan weaving is actually sold, and it holds the Lami-Lamihan Festival in June — the week when Yakan dress, weaving, music and horsemanship are all on display at once.
The Datu Kalun shrine in town commemorates the leader who founded the settlement, and the market is the working heart of the place.
Yakan textile is the thing to buy and to understand: dense geometric weaving in tight color, structurally unlike the ikat and the malong found elsewhere in the region.
before_you_go: Reached by ferry from Zamboanga City.
Coordinate through the city tourism office; this is normal practice on Basilan rather than an unusual precaution.
June for the festival, if the timing works.
items.getting_there: By sea from Zamboanga City: fastcraft go direct to Lamitan (PHP 150 in 2018) and conventional ferries take about 1 hour 30 minutes. Lamitan is about 45 minutes by road from Isabela City. Contact the City Tourism Office before arriving; in 2018 it ran a tour with guide, escort and van for PHP 400 a head.
items.best_time: The Lami-Lamihan Festival, held around June 29, the Feast of Saints Peter and Paul.

items.name: Bulingan Falls
items.summary: A short drive out of Lamitan, and the island’s best-known waterfall.
detail: A broad curtain falling into a pool in forest outside Lamitan, and the standard day trip from the city. It is a local swimming spot as much as an attraction, busiest at weekends.
The setting — rubber and forest on a green volcanic island — is as much the experience as the falls themselves.
before_you_go: Go with a local contact or through the tourism office rather than making your own way.
Fuller and more dramatic in the wet months; the pool is better for swimming when it is not.
items.getting_there: By road through rubber plantations on the Limook–Balobo–Bulingan road, a little over 30 minutes from Isabela City. If you are only going to the falls, take the fastcraft from Zamboanga to Lamitan and go first to the City Tourism Office, which arranges transport and guides.
items.best_time: After a few dry days: the morning after heavy rain in 2021 the water ran murky, while in a dry spell in August 2018 the flow was gentle.

do.title: See the column-like rock formations
do.detail: The falls are less than 10 metres high but wide, and the water drops over rocks that look like stone posts set side by side.

do.title: Swim in the pool below the falls
do.detail: The edges have been cemented and part of the runoff held back to form a pool, which is busiest at weekends and better for swimming outside the wet months.

do.title: Go on to Calugusan Beach
do.detail: Visitors usually combine the falls with a swim at Calugusan Beach in the same city; coordinate with the city tourism office first.

items.name: Malamawi Island
items.municipality: Isabela City (Region IX) — crossed to from Basilan
items.summary: A white-sand beach a short boat ride off Isabela.
detail: Malamawi lies across a narrow channel from Isabela and carries the island’s best-known beach — white sand, shallow water, and close enough that the crossing is a few minutes rather than an expedition.
It is the standard weekend outing for Basilan and Zamboanga residents, which means it is busy on Sundays and quiet the rest of the week.
before_you_go: The crossing is by pump boat from Isabela City, which is administratively in Region IX rather than BARMM — the island is listed here because a traveler on Basilan will be told to go, and the boundary is invisible on the ground.
Facilities are basic. Bring water and food.
Most people swim covered here.
items.getting_there: Fly to Zamboanga, take a Canelar jeepney to Plaza Pershing near the port, then a fastcraft to Isabela City (45 minutes to an hour). Outrigger boats beside Isabela port cross in about 5 minutes (PHP 5 shared or PHP 100 for the whole boat in 2018), and habal-habal drivers at the landing take you 15 to 20 minutes to the white beach in Barangay Lukbuton (PHP 50).

eat.title: Peanuts from Interco
eat.detail: An Isabela peanut shop with no sign, known locally as Interco, sells roasted and adobo peanuts and peanut butter and often sells out before 5 pm.

items.name: Calugusan Beach
items.summary: A white-sand public beach in Lamitan, a short drive from Bulingan Falls.
detail: Calugusan is a barangay of Lamitan with a strip of white sand on the coast. It is the usual swim after a visit to Bulingan Falls.

At low tide broken shells and coral cover the public beach, and a writer who visited in 2015 found it deserted. A gated private beach less than a kilometre further on is cleaner, with clearer water and a small wharf.
before_you_go: Coordinate with the Lamitan city tourism office before visiting.
Bring water and shade; the noon sun is hard on an empty beach.
items.getting_there: By road from Lamitan city or Bulingan Falls; turn into Barangay Calugusan and follow the road past houses and farmland to the shore.
items.best_time: Avoid high noon, when the sand glares and the heat is fierce; at low tide broken shells and coral cover the shore.

do.title: Swim at the public white-sand beach
do.detail: At low tide broken shells and coral cover the shore, and the noon sun is hard, so bring water and shade.

do.title: Watch the jumps off the small wharf
do.detail: Local young people jump from the small wharf into deep water between the public beach and the gated private beach, less than 1 km further on, where the water is clearer.

items.name: Basilan National Park
items.summary: The forested heart of Basilan, dominated by Basilan Peak at around 971 metres.
detail: Basilan National Park covers the eastern part of the island's remaining public forest, between Isabela City and the municipalities of Lamitan, Tipo-Tipo and Sumisip. Its highest point is Basilan Peak.
The Yakan's old name for the island, Uleyan, comes from this peak, which traders crossing the Celebes Sea used as a landmark.
It is one of the few densely forested areas left in the province, with many endemic species.

Basilan's highest point, Punu Ulayan, rises to about 1,000 metres and is the highest point in the Sulu Archipelago. Long a passage for the Abu Sayyaf, it was opened to hikers with the first official climb on 14 September 2025, after Basilan was declared free of the group; hikers are advised to arrange a vehicle to the trailhead, make a courtesy call at the military camp and register through the provincial tourism office.
before_you_go: Most of Basilan's interior is still not visitor country. Climb only as the 2025 parties did, through the provincial tourism office and the military; otherwise locals advise staying in the town centres and seeing the peak from Lamitan or from the sea.
items.getting_there: The peak is visible from the Basilan Strait and from Lamitan.

do.detail: Locals advise visitors to stay in the city centres rather than go into the interior, so view the park's forested peak from a distance.

do.title: Climb Punu Ulayan from Mahatalang
do.detail: The trail starts at about 600 metres on a rough road in Mahatalang, Sumisip, and follows an old logging path into forest; the first official party took just over 2.5 hours up and about an hour down.

do.title: Look for pitcher plants above 800 metres
do.detail: Higher up the forest turns mossy, with pitcher plants, sunbirds and the Zamboanga bulbul.

do.title: Respect the grave on the second summit
do.detail: The first summit is marked by a giant tree and the slightly higher second one by the grave of a village ancestor; keep it quiet, and bring no alcohol.

items.name: Datu Kalun Shrine and Museum of Lamitan
items.summary: A park honouring Lamitan's founder, and the museum of the Lami-Lamihan festival.
detail: The Datu Kalun Shrine is a triangular park in the heart of downtown Lamitan, built as a tribute to Pedro Cuevas, known as Datu Kalun, who took over leadership from the native chieftains and founded the settlement in 1886, and is remembered as a Yakan leader.
The Museum of Lamitan shows the colour of the Lami-Lamihan festival and the Yakan's traditional textiles, and doubles as the town's information centre.
before_you_go: Coordinate with the city tourism office, which is normal practice on Basilan.
items.getting_there: In downtown Lamitan.
items.best_time: Around June 29, for the Lami-Lamihan Festival.

do.title: See the Yakan textiles in the Museum of Lamitan
do.detail: The museum shows colourful, intricate traditional Yakan textiles and highlights from the Lami-Lamihan festival.

do.title: Pick up information at the museum
do.detail: The museum also serves as the town's information centre.

do.title: Walk the triangular park downtown
do.detail: The shrine is a triangular park in the centre of downtown Lamitan, built in honour of the Yakan leader Datu Kalun.

items.name: Monte Santo Shrine
items.summary: A Catholic pilgrimage shrine on Mount Ubit, walked as the Stations of the Cross in Holy Week.
detail: The shrine stands atop Mount Ubit in Lamitan. Devout Catholics climb to it during Holy Week to walk the Stations of the Cross.
It is a reminder that Lamitan has a large Christian population alongside its Yakan and Muslim neighbours.
before_you_go: A place of worship. Dress modestly and keep quiet during prayers.
Coordinate with the city tourism office.
items.best_time: Holy Week, when pilgrims walk the Stations of the Cross.

do.title: Walk the Stations of the Cross up Mount Ubit in Holy Week
do.detail: Devout Catholics climb to the shrine in Holy Week; dress modestly, keep quiet during prayers, and coordinate with the city tourism office.

items.name: Fort Pikit
items.summary: An 1893 Spanish stone fort on a hilltop, a National Historical Landmark since 2012.
detail: The Spanish built Fort Pikit in 1893 during their campaign against the Moro. It has two towers fitted for artillery and a rubble wall 38 metres on each side, and was meant to hold an officer, 60 infantrymen and 6 artillerymen.

It changed hands again and again: the Americans took it in 1902, then the Philippine Constabulary, the Japanese in the Second World War and the Allies after them. The Philippine Army and later the Marines used it until 2007.

The National Historical Commission declared it a National Historical Landmark in 2012. Its barangays voted to join the Bangsamoro in 2019, and since 2024 the fort lies in the new municipality of Malidegao in the Special Geographic Area.
before_you_go: Ruins: watch your footing on the walls and do not climb loose masonry.
items.getting_there: On a hill at the back of the Pikit Municipal Hall, facing the national highway.

items.name: Adlaw Pagtabuh-tabuh
items.summary: A weekly Saturday market in Panglima Sugala where Badjao fishers and Tausug farmers still trade goods by barter.
detail: Every Saturday, Badjao fishers bring fish, dried octopus, seaweed and shells to the shore at Panglima Sugala, and farmers from the mainland arrive with cassava, bananas, coconuts, sugarcane and other produce. Most trade is a direct exchange of seafood for farm goods.
The market is busy by 6 am and most produce is sold or traded before 9 am. Buyers come from Bongao, Sapa-Sapa, Simunul and Sitangkai, and visitors with nothing to trade can pay in cash.
There are no cash registers, price tags or weighing scales. The Bangsamoro Information Office calls it one of the few places in the Philippines where barter trade is still a working tradition.

eat.title: Marang off the carts
eat.detail: Shoppers crowd round the carts of freshly harvested marang on market day.

eat.title: Cowfish and seaweed by the tumpok
eat.detail: Goods are sold in heaps rather than by weight: in 2022, 2 heaps of gamay or lato seaweed cost PHP 100 and about 8 taballung (cowfish) PHP 150.

eat.title: Tausug sweets from the Batu-Batu stores
eat.detail: Small stores at Batu-Batu market sometimes sell bawlo, junay, putli mandih and other Tawi-Tawi delicacies.

before_you_go: The island is privately run; one 2022 itinerary paid PHP 100 per person to land.
Boat hire for a day of island hopping costs PHP 9,000 to 15,000, so it is cheaper in a group.
items.getting_there: By hired boat from Bongao, often combined with Simunul and Panampangan Island.
items.best_time: Late afternoon: as the island closest to Bongao it works best as the last stop of a boat day, in time for the sunset.

do.title: Swim off the boardwalk
do.detail: The boardwalk crosses shallow water to the white beach, and large fish can be seen beside it.

do.title: Add it to a Simunul and Panampangan boat day
do.detail: A 2022 itinerary reached Sangay Siapo at 4:30 pm after Panampangan and Simunul and was back in Bongao by early evening.

do.title: Watch the sunset with Bongao in view
do.detail: From the island you can see parts of the capital across the water as the sun goes down.

items.name: Sangay Siapo Island
items.summary: A small white-sand resort island near Bongao with a boardwalk and shallow, clear water.
detail: Sangay Siapo is a privately owned resort island with overwater cottages linked by a boardwalk. Large fish gather on one side of the boardwalk, and the water around the island is shallow.
It is usually visited on a boat day from Bongao together with Simunul and Panampangan Island. Photos on Wikimedia Commons place it in Simunul; travel guides describe it only as near Bongao.

before_you_go: It is a working government building; ask at the gate before walking in.
items.getting_there: By tricycle from downtown Bongao; tricycles can be hired for a half-day or full-day tour of the island.
items.best_time: Late September, for Kamahardikaan, the founding anniversary of the province (separated from Sulu on 27 September 1973), when decorated lepa fleets sailed off Bongao on 24 September 2023; the Agal-Agal seaweed festival falls on 25 September.

do.title: Go after the Bud Bongao climb
do.detail: One 2022 itinerary came down from Bud Bongao at 6 pm and visited the capitol at 7 pm.

do.title: Look over Bongao Port from the waterfront
do.detail: From the port the capitol shows near the centre of the skyline with Bud Bongao behind it.

items.name: Tawi-Tawi Provincial Capitol
items.summary: The seat of the provincial government, on a hill over Bongao, with a large dome and minarets modelled on the province's mosques.
detail: The capitol stands on a hill in Barangay Tubig-Boh that looks over the town and the nearby islands. Its large dome and minarets take their design from the mosques of the province.
Travel guides list it among the sights of Bongao, usually on the same day as Bud Bongao and a walk through the downtown.

eat.title: Pic-a-Pie in Tubig-Boh
eat.detail: Pic-a-Pie Restaurant is in Tubig-Boh, the capitol's barangay, open 9 am to 5:30 pm.

eat.title: Coffee at Sameera's
eat.detail: A 2022 group stopped at Sameera's in town for coffee at about PHP 40 each.

before_you_go: It is a private resort; one 2022 itinerary paid PHP 100 per person to enter.
items.getting_there: In Barangay Bahod, Bongao, about 3 km from Sanga-Sanga Airport (from a search snippet of a MindaNews photo post); reached by tricycle.
items.best_time: Late afternoon, for the sunset.

do.title: Watch the sunset from the beach
do.detail: Guides to Bongao suggest ending the day here for the sunset.

do.title: Look at the clam-shell architecture
do.detail: The buildings follow the smooth curves of a giant clam's shell.
